input:
This proposal sets out an exciting opportunity to install a rooftop solar array, a project that would allow the site to generate its own clean electricity, reduce its exposure to energy prices, and take a meaningful step on its wider sustainability journey. The headline figures are a capital cost of $1673k, appraised over a 15-year horizon, and the ask at this stage is approval to proceed to detailed design, so that the project can move forward with confidence while the remaining questions are worked through in a structured way.

Case
The roof is currently unused, and the site buys all of its electricity for daytime operation. A rooftop array generates during the hours when the site load is present, so the case rests primarily on self-consumption: generated energy displaces purchased energy at the point of use, and no export income is assumed in the appraisal, which keeps the case prudent. Export is treated as incidental, because export prices are set outside the project, and a case built on them would rest on a term the project does not control. The roof is the one surface on the site that can hold generation without taking land from operations, parking, or storage, and generation on the roof avoids the cable runs and ground works of a ground-mounted array on a site with no spare ground, making it a natural fit overall.
It is worth noting that the condition of the roof covering and the load capacity of the structure are not yet fully established at proposal stage, and the case is written on the basis that detailed design confirms both before any installation is committed. A roof that needs early replacement would change the sequence, because panels fixed over a covering near the end of its life would be lifted and refitted at the first re-roofing; the survey at detailed design will state the remaining life of the covering and the installation will be planned against it. Access for installation and for later maintenance is also part of the case: a system that cannot be reached safely for cleaning, inspection, and repair will lose output over its life, and the access route is designed with the array rather than after it, ensuring that the installation remains maintainable throughout its life.

Generation and load fall in the same hours on most days the site operates, and this match is, in many ways, the load-bearing assumption behind the whole case. A site whose load peaked outside daylight hours would export most of what the array generates, and the same installation would return a quite different result on the same capital. The daytime pattern at this site is measured rather than assumed, and detailed design will test the layout against the metered profile, including the low-load days when generation can exceed the load and the surplus passes to export at the incidental value the appraisal allows it.

Costs
The capital cost is $1673k. This figure covers the modules, the inverters, the mounting system, cabling and switchgear, metering, access and scaffolding for the installation works, and the design and approval costs of the stages that follow this decision. No contractor is named at this stage, and the figure is a proposal-stage estimate built from the surveyed roof area and current supply prices; detailed design will replace it with priced items against a fixed layout, and the construction decision will be taken on the detailed figure, not on this one. The appraisal horizon is the period over which the installation is expected to generate without major component replacement beyond the inverter reserve carried in operating costs.
Operating costs are the costs of keeping the array in service: periodic cleaning where soiling is found to reduce output, inspection of fixings and cabling, monitoring of generation against expectation, and a reserve for inverter replacement within the horizon. Generation displaces purchases, and the saving in any year is the displaced energy valued at the tariff the site would otherwise pay; the appraisal states the saving on that basis and does not capitalise export. The result is sensitive to two terms that detailed design can narrow but not entirely remove: the share of generation the site consumes as it is generated, and the tariff path over the horizon. A lower self-consumption share sends more energy to export at a lower value, and the appraisal is therefore stated on the consumption pattern measured at the site rather than on a generic profile, which gives a more robust basis for the decision.

It should also be noted that the estimate is a proposal-stage figure and is labelled as such wherever it is used. Prices for modules and inverters move between proposal and procurement, and the construction proposal will restate the capital on the prices then current rather than defending this figure. Work the survey may bring forward — renewal of the roof covering, strengthening of the structure — is not inside the capital figure: if detailed design finds such work necessary, it will be priced and reported as enabling work with its own justification, because a roof renewal serves the building whether or not the array proceeds.

Schedule
Work starts one quarter after approval. The first stage is detailed design: the structural survey, the roof condition survey, the electrical design, and the layout are completed and the grid connection application is submitted on the designed capacity. Procurement follows design freeze, because module and inverter selection fixes the mounting design and the cable routes; ordering before freeze would buy equipment against a layout that may still change, creating avoidable risk. Installation is phased so that roof sections are taken in turn and the site stays in operation, with each phase closed, tested, and connected before the next begins. Commissioning covers protection settings, metering, and monitoring, and handover includes the operating instructions, the maintenance schedule, and the as-built records, ensuring a smooth transition into operation.
The schedule risk sits in two places. The grid connection terms can set conditions that change the electrical design, and a late answer would extend the design stage. Weather governs roof work, and the installation phases carry float for lost days rather than a compressed programme that assumes continuous access. Neither risk is priced as a contingency line in the capital figure; both will be reported at the construction decision with the design-stage findings, so that decision-makers have a complete picture.

Approvals run inside the design stage rather than after it. The connection application, the structural sign-off, and the roof warranty position are each settled on the designed layout, and each can return conditions; the programme holds the installation start until the conditions are known, because starting installation against unsettled conditions risks a built array that cannot be connected, or a covering warranty voided by the fixings. The float for lost weather days sits in the installation phases, where the weather acts, rather than in the design stage, where it does not, ensuring the programme remains realistic.

Decision requested
The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design. The capital projects team owns the detailed design stage and will report back with the survey findings, the fixed layout, the grid connection terms, and a priced construction proposal. No construction commitment is made by this approval, and no contractor is appointed under it. If the surveys return findings that change the case — a roof covering at the end of its life, a structure that cannot carry the array without strengthening, or connection terms that restrict export below the incidental level assumed — the construction proposal will state the change and the case will be reappraised before a construction decision is asked, ensuring that every step is taken on a sound footing.
